title: BEAR: Diagnosing Embodied Skills in Multimodal Models
one_liner: Break embodied robot tasks into 14 atomic skills to diagnose which specific abilities a vision-language model is missing, then patch weak perception with external tools.
lead: Robot instruction-following relies on a multimodal language model—one that reads images, video, and text—to understand its world and decide what to do next. But when it fails on a full task, you cannot tell whether the failure came from poor seeing, poor reasoning, or poor planning. BEAR solves this by cutting tasks into 14 small, named skills, testing each one separately, so you discover exactly which capability needs fixing.

problem.h2: Black-box task failure hides the real bottleneck
paras: Today's robot task evaluation is simple: give the model a long instruction like "pick up the apple and place it in the sink", let it run start to finish, and mark pass or fail. But this hides the actual problem. If it fails, you know the final outcome was wrong, but not why. Did it fail because it could not see the apple clearly? Or did it see the apple but misunderstand the sequence of steps it should take? Or did it plan the steps correctly but estimate positions wrong when trying to place the apple? Without knowing which specific ability broke, you cannot fix it.

A beginner might try giving the model a chain-of-thought prompt—asking it to reason step by step—or using a bigger model with longer compute time. But this does not work because the fundamental problem is not reasoning about what to do; it is that the model lacks a specific foundational skill, like accurate spatial reasoning from a first-person view or stable tracking of an object across video frames. Patch reasoning and you still fail; the bottleneck remains.

callout.html: Evaluate models by testing 14 small, specific skills separately instead of whole task success, so bottlenecks become visible.

steps.text: Gather 4,469 real and simulated robot interactions: images, video frames, text instructions.
Break each long task into 14 atomic steps—each step is one focused question, each answerable by testing one small capability.
Run 20 different multimodal language models; grade each on its own small skill question, not the whole task.
Chart which skills are weak across many models; find that perception (seeing, locating, tracking) fails before reasoning (planning, predicting steps).

Give the model external help: visual detectors identify objects, spatial reasoners compute positions. This works because the bottleneck was missing information—once the model receives exact positions from the detector instead of relying on its weak vision encoding, it can plan correctly.

object.h2: What the paper changes: task structure
paras: Instead of feeding a robot model one long task and marking pass or fail, the paper restructures the evaluation: each embodied task becomes a sequence of 14 small, independent questions, each testing one narrow skill. A single high-level instruction—'pick up the apple and place it in the sink'—becomes a chain of vision-and-reasoning questions: "Where is the apple?" (localization), "What is the next step?" (reasoning), "Draw the bounding box on the apple" (spatial), "Predict the trajectory to the sink" (planning), and so on. Each question is graded separately.

hidden.h2: The capability bottleneck: which skill is weakest
hidden.name: skill-specific failure rate
paras: The hidden quantity is the performance of each model on each of the 14 skills—measured simply as the fraction of questions answered correctly on that skill across all test samples. Because the paper tests each skill independently, differences in failure rate between skills become visible. A model that answers 85% of perception questions correctly but only 40% of trajectory-reasoning questions reveals that perception is the bottleneck, not reasoning.

The paper measures this using a hierarchical diagnosis framework: organize the 14 skills into categories (low-level perception, high-level reasoning, spatial understanding, temporal understanding), then compare failure rates within and across categories. When you see that every model's perception-skill accuracy drops by 30 percentage points compared to its instruction-understanding accuracy, you have identified the bottleneck—and you know exactly where to invest in fixing the model.

heat.caption: Darker means lower accuracy; red border highlights weakest perception skills.

reads.html: The bottleneck is whichever skill the model gets wrong most often. If every model struggles with spotting objects in first-person video but reasons fine, then perception is the limit, because no reasoning can overcome incomplete or wrong visual input—you cannot plan a path to a location you cannot see.

The paper diagnoses via hierarchical skill-level evaluation: decompose task-level outcomes into per-skill accuracy metrics, compute the gap between best and worst skill per model, and observe that perceptual skills (localization, tracking, spatial) consistently rank lowest.

mechanism.h2: Why breaking tasks into skills reveals bottlenecks
paras: Whole-task evaluation collapses all failure modes into a single pass-or-fail. If a model fails at "pick up the apple and place it in the sink", the failure could come from any of its ten sub-steps: maybe it did not see the apple, or it forgot the instruction, or it planned correctly but miscalculated the position of the sink. You have one bit of information (failed) but ten possible causes. When you test the same model on a narrow skill—just "locate the apple in this image"—you isolate the cause. If it fails at localization but succeeds at instruction-following, you know the bottleneck is perception, not reasoning. The skill-level structure forces a diagnosis.

Once you know the bottleneck is weak perception, you can augment the model with external tools: a visual detector that finds objects without relying on the language model's built-in visual encoding, a spatial reasoner that computes exact positions. Adding these tools does not change the language model's reasoning; it changes the inputs the reasoning engine receives—from noisy, incomplete visual information to rich, precise cues. The model then does better planning because it is working from cleaner perceptual data.

stages.s: Full long-horizon task; image, video, instruction
Augment model with tools for weak skills
Higher accuracy on full tasks, because weak skills have been fixed

math.words: For each model and each skill, accuracy is the count of correct answers divided by the total number of test samples for that skill. The bottleneck is the skill with the lowest accuracy.
symbols: fraction of correct answers on one skill (0 to 1)
number of right answers the model gave for that skill
number of test questions for that skill

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Model X on Localization: 34 correct out of 40 samples → accuracy = 34/40 = 0.85 (85%)
Model X on Trajectory: 28 correct out of 40 samples → accuracy = 28/40 = 0.70 (70%)
Model X on Instruction: 36 correct out of 40 samples → accuracy = 36/40 = 0.90 (90%)
Bottleneck: Trajectory reasoning is the weakest link (70% < 85% < 90%), so focus on improving trajectory prediction.

math.note: The gap between skills reveals where the model struggles most; bigger gaps mean clearer bottlenecks.

bars.h2: Impact of skill-level diagnosis plus tool augmentation

charts.title: Unaided model (whole-task eval)

items.html: If the 14 skills are not truly separable—for example, if "trajectory prediction" is impossible without first solving "localization"—then testing them separately gives false accuracy numbers. The paper must carefully design each skill so it can be answered with the given information alone.
A visual detector trained for kitchen tasks may not work for warehouse navigation. Each new embodied domain may require retraining the augmentation tools, limiting generality.
Once you fix perception with tools, the bottleneck may move to reasoning or planning. The paper measures improvement but does not guarantee a single diagnosis applies to all future tasks.

Choose skills that truly isolate one capability each; design test samples so each skill can be solved given only the information relevant to that skill; validate that augmenting the weakest skill in isolation produces visible improvement on full tasks.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small version of BEAR: collect five embodied episodes (pick-and-place tasks, for example) from a simulator. Decompose each into three key skills: object localization, next-step reasoning, and trajectory planning. For one multimodal model, test it on each of the 15 questions (five episodes times three skills). Record the accuracy for each skill. Then augment the model with a simple tool: a pretrained object detector that provides bounding boxes of all relevant objects. Re-test the same model on the same 15 questions. The demo should show (1) a clear gap in accuracy between skills—some skills weaker than others—because if you see the model succeed at reasoning but fail at localization, the whole-task test cannot tell you that; skill-level testing does. And (2) a measurable boost in accuracy on the weakest skill after augmentation, because the detector removes the perception bottleneck, unblocking reasoning.
demo.metric_eq: skill_bottleneck_gap = highest_skill_accuracy - lowest_skill_accuracy; post_augment_gain = unaided_weak_skill_accuracy - augmented_weak_skill_accuracy
demo.closing: The demo makes it undeniable that isolating skills exposes bottlenecks that whole-task evaluation hides, because any one weak link in a long chain of steps will collapse the whole task, so only skill-level diagnosis tells you which link is actually broken.
